To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

for continuous messages with a length of 1 kbyte and a line utilization of 20%, packet switching is more cost-effective for distances of up to 500 km and circuit switching is more attractive for distances above 1,500 km.
for continuous traffic patterns, circuit switching is more cost-effective for short message lengths and for intermittent traffic patterns for long message lengths.

the boundary between circuit and packet switching is governed by: (a) the message length; (b) the traffic pattern (continuous or intermittent messages); (c) the network load; (d) the distance; (e) the intermessage interval; (f) the length of dialogue; and (g) the kind of switching processor used.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a comparison of packet and circuit switching techniques from the point of view of delay performance and dynamic costs.

the question of whether packet switching can be used as a substitute for circuit switching in data networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

packet switching is the more cost-effective technique for the following cases: (i) for intermittent message streams, and (ii) for continuous message streams, if the message length is small and/or if the line utilization is high.
circuit switching is the most efficient technique for the handling of continuous messages and packet switching is most efficient for the handling of intermittent messages.
packet switching has a clear advantage for short and long messages and for intermittent traffic, whereas circuit switching is better for continuous traffic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
packet switching can be more efficient than circuit switching for a wide range of traffic patterns and message lengths if the network usage cost per bit is sufficiently low.
the packet-switching technique is most attractive when the message lengths are small and the traffic pattern is characterized by a high proportion of no-data intervals.

packet switching is the more attractive alternative for the following cases: - when the traffic is of the intermittent type, i.e., the message blocks are intersperesed with idle intervals, and/or - when the messages are long, i.e. the average message block length is greater than 1000 bits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
packet switching has a definite advantage in the area of intermittent traffic.
the cost-performance trade-off is not as simple as one might expect.

packet switching can be used to provide a cost-effective solution to the delay problem of circuit switching, provided the traffic is intermittent, the message length is small and the network utilization is low.
